findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.
Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging gait and distractibility; observed event with side-to-side head shaking and closed eyes
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs and observe an event
action_criteria.rationale: Two weeks of right leg weakness and daily shaking events: the diagnosis rests on positive signs such as the Hoover sign and collapsing weakness and on the semiology of an observed event, not on the exclusion of other disease (DSM-5 criterion B).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Habitual events recorded on video with no EEG change and a normal interictal record
action_criteria.label: Record the habitual events on video-EEG
action_criteria.rationale: She was started on levetiracetam empirically for these events. Recording her habitual events without ictal change reaches the ILAE documented level of certainty and assesses co-occurring epilepsy before the drug is withdrawn, as the AAN guideline advises.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No lesion explaining the right leg weakness
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI without contrast, once, if a structural question remains
action_criteria.rationale: The leg weakness began suddenly and the urgent care CT was normal; preserved reflexes, flexor plantars and the positive signs already answer the structural question, so a single non-contrast scan is defensible but does not contribute to the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Levetiracetam started for the events and as-needed lorazepam identified for supervised withdrawal; no pharmacokinetic interactions
action_criteria.label: Review the medicines started for the events, including levetiracetam and lorazepam
action_criteria.rationale: Levetiracetam was started empirically for her events without effect and can worsen mood in a patient treated for depression and anxiety, and she takes lorazepam as needed. Once the events are recorded, the review sets up the levetiracetam taper and the benzodiazepine plan.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment, if it will guide therapy
action_criteria.rationale: It can quantify her anxiety, mood and trauma-related symptoms to target psychological treatment, but it does not make the diagnosis and is the most expensive item on this pathway, so it is justified only when the result will shape therapy.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Background evidence only, with no bearing on this patient's work-up
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Reading on positive signs and treatment trials is background knowledge, not a clinical step; nothing in this patient's diagnosis or plan depends on it.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat CT after the normal urgent care scan, repeat MRI, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Start or escalate antiseizure medication for the functional seizures, or stop it abruptly.
Give benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (mixed: functional right leg weakness and functional seizures) based on the right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility, and on the three habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid generalized anxiety disorder and depression.
Taper and stop levetiracetam under neurological supervision, since the events are functional and there is no evidence of epilepsy.

Give the patient, family and ward a written plan for typical events: keep safe, do not restrain, wait for the event to end, and do not give emergency benzodiazepines or intubate for a typical functional seizure.
Do not use her as-needed lorazepam to abort the events; review it with her psychiatrist and taper it gradually as her anxiety treatment allows.

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no syncope, palpitations or chest pain, and the events are shaking with retained awareness; an ECG adds nothing.
No murmur, syncope or embolic question is raised; an echocardiogram answers nothing in this patient.
She is aware during the shaking and has no syncope or palpitations; nothing suggests an arrhythmia.
A head CT at the outside urgent care during this illness was normal; repeating it answers no new question and adds radiation.
She is afebrile with no infection, inflammatory or encephalopathic feature; a lumbar puncture would add iatrogenic risk and answer no question.
FDG-PET has no diagnostic role in functional seizures or functional weakness and answers no question in this patient.

The right leg weakness has normal reflexes, tone and bulk with a positive Hoover sign and collapsing weakness; it is not neuromuscular, and a normal EMG would only feed the search for an organic cause.
Sensory loss of the whole right leg ending at the inguinal crease, with intact vibration and proprioception, is not a question about the somatosensory pathway.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder (conversion disorder) with right leg weakness and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures

differential.key_features: Daily shaking events treated empirically with levetiracetam, with no change. Habitual events recorded on video-EEG without ictal change; co-occurring epilepsy remains possible in about one in five patients with functional seizures.

Sudden right leg heaviness at work raises an anterior cerebral artery territory stroke; symmetric reflexes, flexor plantars, a positive Hoover sign with collapsing weakness and a dragging gait without circumduction argue against it.

differential.diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis or another structural lesion of the brain or spinal cord
differential.key_features: Leg weakness with sensory loss in a young adult raises demyelination or a cord lesion; normal reflexes and tone, flexor plantars, intact vibration and proprioception and the positive functional signs are incompatible with a corticospinal or dorsal column lesion.

key_clinical_evidence: The right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility are validated rule-in signs; the inguinal sensory boundary and the tubular field are supportive only.
Three habitual events (asynchronous limb shaking with side-to-side head movements and closed eyes) were recorded on video-EEG without ictal change: the ILAE documented level of certainty.
Levetiracetam was started empirically without effect on the events; with the events recorded and no evidence of epilepsy it is tapered and stopped, and it may worsen her mood meanwhile.
Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for functional seizures; her as-needed lorazepam should not be used to abort the events (AAN 2025).
The recent separation, financial worry and earlier functional left arm numbness in college are supportive context; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Generalized anxiety disorder, recurrent major depression and childhood emotional abuse
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset shortly after separating from her partner of five years
red_herrings.intended_effect: Make the diagnosis from the stressor alone, without positive signs or recorded events

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: An empirical start is not a diagnosis: the events did not change on levetiracetam, and the habitual events recorded without ictal change support a supervised taper.
red_herrings.data_point: Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily started empirically at urgent care for suspected seizures
red_herrings.intended_effect: Take the antiseizure drug as evidence of epilepsy and continue or escalate it

sequence_constraints.reason: The decision to taper antiseizure drugs rests on the recorded events (AAN 2025; Oto 2005).

findings.result: Right hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during left hip flexion against resistance.
Right hip flexion, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion reach 4/5 and then collapse suddenly.
Right leg dragged behind with the hip externally rotated, without circumduction.
The gait briefly normalizes when she turns to look behind her.
Two minutes of asynchronous, waxing and waning limb movements with side-to-side head shaking and the eyes closed; she was verbally responsive during the event and had no confusion afterwards.

Light-touch and pinprick loss over the whole right leg sharply demarcated at the inguinal crease, and a tubular right visual field on confrontation not tested at two distances; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes 2+ and symmetric with flexor plantars; normal tone, no pronator drift; vibration and proprioception intact.
findings.sign: Reflexes, tone and posterior column sensation

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: right Hoover sign, collapsing weakness, dragging monoplegic gait and distractibility of the right leg deficit. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion. The event semiology (asynchronous waxing and waning movements, side-to-side head shaking, eyes closed, retained responsiveness, no postictal confusion) is typical of functional seizures; the examination does not by itself exclude epileptic seizures.

interactions: Sertraline with lorazepam: additive central nervous system depression; minor.
Levetiracetam: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interactions with the other medicines.
current_medications.proposed: Sertraline 100 mg once daily; lorazepam 0.5 mg as needed, up to twice daily; dicyclomine 20 mg four times daily as needed; levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily
current_medications.summary: No pharmacokinetic interactions; levetiracetam carries mood and behavioral cautions, and lorazepam carries benzodiazepine cautions.
warnings: Levetiracetam: behavioral adverse effects (irritability, low mood, anxiety) are common, and a history of depression is a labelled caution; when it is discontinued, reduce the dose gradually rather than stopping abruptly.

Lorazepam: sedation, tolerance and dependence; avoid using a benzodiazepine as rescue for paroxysmal events not shown to be epileptic, and after regular use taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly.
Dicyclomine: anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, dizziness), additive with sedatives.

activating_procedures.hyperventilation: Performed for 3 minutes. No significant change in background. No epileptiform discharges provoked. Did not trigger a clinical event.
activating_procedures.photic_stimulation: Performed at flash frequencies 1-30 Hz. Normal photic driving response. No photoparoxysmal response.

artifacts.description: Prominent during the events; the underlying background remained discernible.

background.anterior_rhythms: Low-amplitude beta activity, symmetric, mildly increased
background.overall: Continuous inpatient video-EEG for 48 hours, international 10-20 system. Normal, symmetric background in wakefulness and sleep.
background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: 10 Hz alpha rhythm, symmetric, well-organized, reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: Normal sleep architecture with vertex waves, sleep spindles, and K-complexes in stage N2 sleep

findings.morphology: Asynchronous shaking of all four limbs with side-to-side head movements and the eyes closed, lasting 1 min 50 s; she answered the technologist during the event. Movement artifact; the posterior alpha rhythm remained discernible. No evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.
Waxing and waning limb shaking with the eyes closed, lasting 2 min 35 s. Posterior alpha rhythm persisted between artifact bursts; no evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.
Asynchronous limb shaking with side-to-side head movements, lasting 1 min 10 s. Posterior alpha rhythm persisted; no evolving rhythmic activity and no postictal slowing.

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL video-EEG. Three habitual events were recorded (asynchronous limb shaking with side-to-side head movements and the eyes closed, 1 min 10 s to 2 min 35 s) without ictal EEG change before, during or after the events; the posterior dominant rhythm persisted during the events. No interictal epileptiform discharges. No electrographic seizures.
eeg.limitations: Movement artifact during the events partially obscured some channels.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Defines levels of certainty for psychogenic nonepileptic seizures; the documented level requires a typical event recorded on video-EEG without ictal EEG change.
results.source: LaFrance WC Jr et al. Epilepsia 2013;54:2005-2018

results.finding: For functional seizures: assess for co-occurring epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, taper antiseizure medication without another indication, avoid benzodiazepines, and offer psychological therapy, which is possibly effective.
CBT added to standardised medical care did not reduce dissociative seizure frequency at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured CBT.
results.source: Goldstein LH et al. Lancet Psychiatry 2020;7:491-505

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Guideline and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder, video-EEG confirmation of functional seizures, tapering of unneeded antiseizure drugs and benzodiazepines, and physiotherapy and psychological treatment whose trial effects on primary outcomes were modest.

metadata.teaching_points: This case demonstrates classic functional neurological disorder with both functional weakness (positive Hoover sign, give-way pattern) and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (captured on video-EEG with no ictal correlate). The diagnosis is made by positive signs, not exclusion.

No family history of epilepsy or neurodegenerative disease

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Rachel Donahue is a 28-year-old right-handed woman and elementary school teacher who presents with a two-week history of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of whole-body shaking. The symptoms began abruptly approximately two weeks ago, shortly after she and her partner of five years separated. She was at work when she suddenly noticed her right leg felt heavy and she had difficulty walking. Over the following days the weakness persisted and she began experiencing episodes of generalized shaking. The episodes occur 2-3 times per day, lasting 1-3 minutes each. During these events she reports being aware of her surroundings but unable to control the movements. Witnesses have described the shaking as involving all four limbs with irregular, side-to-side head shaking and intermittent eye closure. There is no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence, and no post-event confusion. Between episodes she has persistent difficulty walking due to the right leg weakness. She has had to take medical leave from her teaching position. She was initially evaluated at an outside urgent care where a CT head was obtained and was reported as normal. She was placed on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily empirically for suspected seizures but reports no change in the frequency or character of the episodes. She was referred for inpatient admission for continuous video-EEG monitoring and further workup. She endorses significant stress related to her recent separation and reports feeling overwhelmed by financial concerns. She has a history of anxiety and depression for which she takes sertraline. She denies any head trauma, fevers, recent infections, or travel. She denies any prior similar episodes, although she does recall a brief period in college where she experienced non-dermatomal numbness in her left arm during a particularly stressful exam period, which resolved spontaneously over several days.

neurological_exam.additional: Hoover sign positive on the right. Give-way pattern on manual muscle testing. Sensory examination shows a non-anatomic distribution with a sharp demarcation at the inguinal crease. During an observed clinical event on the floor (shaking episode lasting 2 minutes), the patient exhibited asynchronous, waxing and waning limb movements with side-to-side head shaking, eyes closed, and was verbally responsive during the event. No post-ictal confusion, no tongue biting, no incontinence.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose normal bilaterally. Heel-to-shin normal on the left. On the right, the patient reports difficulty initiating the movement but when performed, it is smooth and accurate. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive 3mm to 2mm. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no atrophy, no fasciculations.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient walks with a dragging right leg pattern that is inconsistent: the leg is dragged behind with the hip externally rotated, but when distracted (turning to look behind her), the gait briefly normalizes. No circumduction. Tandem gait not performed due to patient's report of imbalance, but she can stand on one leg (left) without difficulty.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. GCS 15. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. No dysarthria. Affect is mildly anxious but cooperative. Attention intact, able to recite months of the year backwards. Recall 3/3 at 5 minutes. No evidence of cognitive impairment.
neurological_exam.motor: Upper extremities: Bulk and tone normal. Strength 5/5 bilaterally in all muscle groups. No pronator drift. Right lower extremity: Give-way weakness noted on formal strength testing. Initial contraction to 4/5 in hip flexors, knee extensors, and ankle dorsiflexors, followed by sudden collapse of effort. On distraction testing (e.g., when asked to lift contralateral leg), involuntary full strength is noted in the affected limb. Left lower extremity: Strength 5/5 throughout. Hoover sign positive on the right: involuntary hip extension on the right is strong when asked to flex the left hip against resistance, but voluntary right hip extension is weak.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the entire right leg, sharply demarcated at the inguinal crease. Proprioception and vibration intact bilaterally in all extremities. Tubular visual field on confrontation testing of right eye noted.
